client: I've been feeling really on edge ever since my partner moved in with me about a month ago. It's hard to explain, but I keep getting this tight feeling in my chest, like I'm constantly waiting for something to go wrong or like I'm losing some part of myself. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: What you're describing — that tightness in your chest, the sense of waiting for something to fall apart — sounds really exhausting to carry, and I can hear in the way you're speaking that there's a lot of tension and urgency beneath these feelings, even if the words themselves feel hard to pin down. It makes a lot of sense that a big life change like moving in together could stir up fears about losing your sense of self or independence, even when the relationship itself is good. I'm really glad you decided to give this a shot, and I want you to know that just naming what's happening is already a meaningful first step — we'll work through this together at whatever pace feels right for you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I mean... it does feel exhausting, you're right about that. But I'm not totally sure it's about losing my independence — it's more like I keep waiting for him to realize I'm not who he thinks I am, like eventually he'll see through me and regret the whole thing. And I guess that's what makes the chest tightness worse, because moving in together just feels like putting us under a microscope where there's nowhere to hide anymore.
therapist: What you're describing — this fear that your partner will eventually "see through" you and be disappointed — has a name in CBT, and it's called an **impostor belief**, and it's more common than you might think, though I can hear how quietly but deeply it's weighing on you right now. It's worth gently asking: what specific evidence do you have that the version of you he's fallen for isn't the *real* you, versus a story your mind has constructed to protect you from vulnerability? Living together doesn't have to be a microscope that exposes your flaws — it can also be the space where someone chooses you *more fully*, and that's a perspective worth exploring together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's true, but it's hard not to feel like the "real" me is the anxious, messy version that I've been carefully keeping hidden from him. Like, he's seen me on good days, patient days, but he hasn't seen me when I'm spiraling at 2am over something small, or when I get so overwhelmed I just shut down completely. I guess my fear is that once he sees all of that up close, every single day, the choice he made when he fell for me won't feel like the same choice anymore.
therapist: I notice you're speaking very quickly, like the thoughts are tumbling out faster than you can catch them, and that urgency makes sense — this fear feels very real and close to the surface right now. But I want to gently challenge something: you're describing your anxious, overwhelmed self as the *hidden real* you, but what if the patient, caring person he fell for is just as real, and what you're actually afraid of is him seeing the *full* picture — which is what intimacy actually requires? The 2am spirals and the shutdown moments aren't the truth beneath the mask; they're just *part* of a whole person, and his choice to love you was never meant to be based on a highlight reel — that's a standard no one could meet.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it feels almost too convenient, like a nice idea that doesn't quite hold up in real life. Because the thing is, he fell for someone who had it mostly together, who was warm and present and fun to be around, and now he's seeing someone who cancels plans and goes silent for days and cries over things she can't even explain. I guess what scares me is that "full picture" intimacy sounds beautiful in theory, but what if his full picture of me just ends up being... too much?
therapist: There's something really striking happening as you speak — your voice is moving very fast and sitting quite high, like part of you is bracing for impact even as you're saying the words, and yet underneath the fear there's also a quiet flicker of something that wants to be convinced otherwise. The question "what if I'm too much?" is one of the most painful a person can carry, but I want to sit with you in this for a moment: the woman who cancels plans, goes silent, and cries without explanation didn't *replace* the warm, present person he fell for — she's been there all along, and he's been loving her without knowing it. That's not a trick or a convenience; that's actually evidence worth examining — because if the "too much" version of you was truly unbearable, it likely would have surfaced in smaller ways already, and he's still here, and he chose to move closer.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me really wants to hold onto that... but then my brain immediately goes, "yeah, but he hasn't seen the worst of it yet." Like, what I've shown him so far feels like the manageable version of my anxiety, not the full spiral where I'm texting him five times in a row at two in the morning because I convinced myself he's pulling away. I guess I'm scared that the evidence you're pointing to only counts up until a certain threshold, and I don't know where that threshold is.
therapist: There's something tender and almost fragile in the way you're saying this — your voice is soft but moving quickly, like you're trying to get the fear out before you lose your nerve, and I want to honor how vulnerable it is to name that specific image: the 2am texts, the spiral, the part of yourself you've kept most carefully out of sight. What I notice is that your mind has set up an unfalsifiable rule — the evidence only counts *until* some unknown threshold — which means no amount of reassurance can ever fully land, because the goalpost can always move to "but he hasn't seen *that* yet." That's not a reflection of reality; that's anxiety doing what anxiety does best — protecting you from hope so you can't be blindsided by loss — and that pattern itself is worth exploring, because you deserve to stop living in waiting for a verdict that may never come.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That thing you said about the goalpost moving... it hit something, because yeah, I do that constantly, I can feel myself doing it even as you describe it. Like as soon as Marcus was kind to me last week, my brain immediately went to "okay but wait until he sees how I get when I'm really scared," and there it goes again. But I guess what I don't know is how to just... stop doing that, because it doesn't feel like a choice I'm making, it feels like the only logical thing to do when you've been caught off guard before.
therapist: The way you just said that — very fast, pitched high, like something cracked open a little — tells me this landed somewhere real, and I want to stay right there with you. You're absolutely right that it doesn't feel like a choice, and that's because this pattern was probably *learned* as protection at some point — when someone important caught you off guard, your mind decided that hope was the dangerous thing, not the threat itself. In CBT we'd call this a safety behavior, and the first step isn't forcing yourself to stop, but learning to notice it with curiosity rather than obedience — the way you just did right now, in real time, which is actually harder and braver than it sounds.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to believe that framing, that it was protection, not weakness. But then another part of me just kind of... deflates, because even if that's true, it doesn't change the fact that I'm still alone, still keeping people at arm's length, still doing the same thing I've apparently always done. Like, okay, so I notice it, I get curious about it, but then what, I'm just supposed to sit there watching myself push people away and feel good about the observation?
therapist: The exhaustion in your voice right now is so clear — you're speaking very fast and your pitch is high, like frustration and grief are both pressing up against each other at once, and I don't want to gloss over that with another reframe, because what you just said deserves to be heard: noticing a pattern without being able to change it yet can feel like being handed a map while your legs are still broken. You're right that awareness alone isn't the destination — but I want to gently push back on one thing: you're not "still alone," you're sitting here talking honestly about your deepest fear with Marcus asleep down the hall, which means something in you is already fighting the pattern, not just watching it. That gap between noticing and changing is exactly where the real work happens, and you don't have to close it alone or all at once.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying about Marcus being down the hall, and part of me wants to hold onto that, but another part just... I don't know, it feels like I'm cheating somehow, like I'm counting on him to fill something that I should be able to fill myself. And honestly, the idea that "the real work happens in the gap" sounds meaningful, but right now that gap just feels like a place where I sit and wait and nothing actually shifts.
therapist: Your voice is moving very fast and sitting very high, but there's something almost flat underneath it, like you're running on fumes — and that combination tells me this isn't just frustration anymore, it's a kind of bone-tired disappointment, maybe even with yourself. I want to gently name something: the belief that you should be able to fill everything yourself, that leaning on Marcus is "cheating," is actually one of the loneliest rules a person can live by, and it might be worth asking where you learned that needing someone else was a failure rather than just... being human. The gap doesn't have to be a waiting room — it can also be the place where we figure out together what "filling it yourself" actually needs to look like, versus the impossibly self-sufficient standard your mind seems to be holding you to.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows you're probably right, but it also feels like... if I start relying on Marcus more, and then something happens, I'll have made myself even more vulnerable than I already am. Like I'll have traded one kind of loneliness for a worse kind. And honestly, I don't even know where I learned that needing people is a failure — it just feels like it's always been there, this voice that says if you can't handle it alone, you're weak.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — very fast, pitched high, like something urgent needs to be said before you lose your nerve — and yet the words themselves carry this quiet, almost resigned weight, like you've been living under that voice for so long you've stopped questioning whether it's actually true. That voice that says "if you can't handle it alone, you're weak" — I want to ask you something gently: whose voice does it actually sound like, because rules that feel like they've "always been there" usually have an origin, someone or something that taught you that needing people was dangerous before you were old enough to decide if you believed it. And here's what strikes me: the very fear you're describing — "if I let Marcus in and lose him, it'll be worse" — is actually proof that connection matters deeply to you, which isn't weakness, it's just a heart that knows what it stands to lose.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I went quiet for a second there, because... yeah, that landed somewhere I wasn't expecting. I think it does sound like my dad, honestly — he used to say things like "figure it out yourself" whenever I came to him upset, like needing comfort was something to be embarrassed about. But I don't know if knowing where it came from actually changes anything, because that voice is still there, still loud, and Marcus is still someone I could lose.
therapist: The quiet before you said that, and the way your voice is moving fast but sitting very high — like something tender just got exposed to the air for the first time — tells me this is one of those moments that matters, and I don't want to rush past it. What your dad taught you wasn't the truth about needing people; it was his limitation, his discomfort with vulnerability, and a child who needed comfort and was turned away learned the only available lesson: *make yourself need less*. Knowing where it came from doesn't silence the voice overnight, but it does mean you can start to hear it as his voice, an old borrowed rule, rather than your own deepest truth — and that's the first crack in the wall.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
